pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, children draw picture graphs (one symbol = one unit) and bar graphs (labelled axes, single-unit scale) with up to four categories, and use a bar graph to solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems (CCSS 2.MD.10). This is the translation between organised counts and a scaled visual, and back again to answer questions — crucially, comparison questions ('how many more votes did cats get than dogs?') that require a difference. Teaching should build the graph from the child's own data, insist on equal-width bars rising from a common baseline read against the scale, and connect reading a value to the count it represents.
bestPractices: Build the graph from data the children collected, mapping each unit to one square/symbol so height means count
Insist on the grammar of a bar graph: equal-width bars, common baseline, evenly spaced, axes labelled, single-unit scale
Read values by tracking the bar top across to the scale, and model comparison as the difference between two bars
Pose put-together (combine two categories), take-apart and compare ('how many more') problems on the finished graph
keyRepresentations: Bar graph with single-unit scale on squared paper
Picture graph with one symbol per unit, aligned in rows
Two bars aligned to show the difference for 'how many more'
Frequency table as the source the graph is drawn from
commonMisconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value instead of the difference between the bars
Reads a bar's value off by one (counts gridlines instead of the value the top reaches, or bars not starting at zero)
Draws bars of unequal width, floating off the baseline, or unevenly spaced, so height no longer means count
Draws picture-graph symbols of different sizes or unaligned, so rows can't be compared by length

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, learners draw picture graphs (one symbol = one unit) and bar graphs (labelled axes, single-unit scale) with up to four categories, then use the finished graph to solve put-together, take-apart and compare ('how many more') problems. The core skill is translating both ways: from organised counts to a scaled visual, and from the visual back to a count that answers a question. Teaching builds the graph from the children's own data, insists on equal-width bars rising from a common baseline read against the scale, and models 'how many more' as the difference (the gap) between two bars rather than the taller bar's value.

activities.title: Build a bar graph from our data on gridded paper
feedback: If a bar doesn't start at zero or floats off the baseline, point out that height can only mean count when every bar starts at the same line; redraw from the baseline.

If a learner reads a value off by one, have them track the bar top straight across to the scale number and check whether they counted gridlines (including the baseline) instead of the value the top reaches.
If bars differ in width, ask what the extra width is supposed to represent; re-establish that only height carries the count, so widths must match.
activities.rationale: Constructing the graph from the learner's own counts, mapping one unit to one square, makes 'height = count' concrete and exposes whether the grammar of a bar graph (equal width, common baseline, labelled single-unit scale) is understood. An optional gridded builder where bars snap to equal width on a baseline can reduce drawing friction, but drawing by hand also surfaces form errors for feedback.

At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable with bar graphs and read them to answer questions about their group; awareness that changing the vertical scale distorts perception begins here
learnerActions: Collect or use a given data set with up to four categories (e.g. favourite pets: cats 9, dogs 6, fish 4, birds 2)
On squared/gridded paper or a gridded canvas, draw one bar per category, shading one square per unit so each bar's height equals its count
Keep every bar the same width, rising from a common baseline (zero line), evenly spaced, and label both axes with a single-unit scale
Read a chosen bar's value back by tracking its top straight across to the scale number, and check it matches the original count
activities.intendedInsight: Height means count: a bar's top read against the scale gives the number of items in that category. This only works if every bar starts from the shared zero baseline. Equal widths keep the bars fair to compare by eye, so that only height carries the count.

activities.title: 'How many more' as the gap between two bars
feedback: If a learner answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value (e.g. 9), align the two bars and count only the squares the taller one sticks up by; name that gap as 'how many more', then re-ask.
If they ask 'how did you get how many more?', check they computed a difference rather than simply reading a height.
For a put-together question, confirm they read both bar values and added them rather than reading one.
For a take-apart question, confirm they read the known part against the scale and took it away from the given total (e.g. 15 − 9 = 6), then checked the result against the other bar.
activities.rationale: The most common error is reporting the taller bar's value for a difference question. Physically aligning the bars and counting the gap gives a visual meaning to subtraction and distinguishes 'how many more' from a single reading. An optional interaction that glides the two bars together and shades the extra squares makes the difference visible, but the subtraction must still be stated.
sourceClaims: Pupils draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems using a bar graph (e.g. 'how many more')
learnerActions: On a finished bar graph, pick two categories and state a comparison question, e.g. 'how many more children chose cats than dogs?'
Line the two bars up side by side and count the squares by which the taller bar sticks up above the shorter one
Write the answer as a subtraction, e.g. cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3, and say in words that 3 is 'how many more'

Repeat with a put-together question ('how many chose cats and dogs together?') and a take-apart question ('15 children chose cats or dogs; use the cats bar to find how many of them did NOT choose cats, then check with the dogs bar') to practise combining and separating counts
activities.intendedInsight: A comparison answer is the difference between two bars (the gap at the top), not the height of the taller bar; put-together and take-apart questions use the same read-the-scale skill with addition or subtraction.

activities.title: Picture graph with uniform, aligned symbols
feedback: If symbols vary in size or rows aren't aligned, ask whether a longer-but-fewer row could look bigger; redraw with equal, aligned symbols.
If a learner gives the longer row's total for 'how many more', line the rows up and count only the extra symbols; name that as the difference, then re-ask.
If a learner miscounts, have them count one symbol per unit and check the total against the data table.
activities.rationale: Picture graphs reinforce one-unit-one-mark and make the need for uniformity and alignment felt, paralleling the equal-width requirement for bars. Keeping 'how many more' as the difference generalises that idea from bars to rows across two representations.
sourceClaims: Pupils draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems using a bar graph (e.g. 'how many more')
learnerActions: Represent the same data as a picture graph, placing exactly one equal-sized symbol per unit in each category's row
Align symbols in rows so the length of a row can be compared at a glance

Read a category's count by counting its symbols, and answer a 'how many more' question by lining up the two rows and counting only the EXTRA symbols in the longer row (the difference, not the longer row's total)
Discuss what goes wrong if symbols are different sizes or not lined up
activities.intendedInsight: Symbols must be uniform and aligned so that a row's length faithfully represents its count; 'how many more' is still the difference between the two counts, read as the extra symbols in the longer row.

activities.title: Check questions: read, compare, and construct
feedback: If the taller-bar answer is chosen, revisit aligning the bars and counting the gap.
If a constructed bar doesn't start at zero, note that a shifted baseline changes the apparent value even when the count is unchanged.
Short-answer or spoken explanation is preferable where possible, since it reveals whether a difference was computed rather than a height read.
activities.rationale: A recognition-only item can check interpretation but does not by itself show independent construction; pairing a comparison item with a construction step exposes whether 'height means count' is truly understood. A wrong answer equal to the taller bar's value targets the specific misconception.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable with bar graphs and read them to answer questions about their group; awareness that changing the vertical scale distorts perception begins here
learnerActions: Answer a 'how many more' multiple-choice or short-answer item where one tempting wrong answer is the taller bar's raw value
Set bar heights (by drawing or dragging a slider) to match given counts, keeping equal width and a zero baseline
Explain in one sentence how you found a difference, so the reasoning (subtraction vs. height) is visible
Answer a scale-awareness prompt: 'if the dogs bar started halfway up, would it still tell us 6? why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means reading values against the scale, computing comparisons as differences, and constructing well-formed bars — all three, not just recognising a correct graph.

constraints: Use the child's own collected data where possible so each unit maps to one square/symbol and height visibly means count.
Insist on the grammar of a bar graph: equal-width bars, common baseline (zero), even spacing, labelled axes, single-unit scale.

A static labelled bar graph or tap-to-reveal annotation is a reference/scaffold only: it can name the parts but does not let the learner construct a graph or compute a comparison, so it cannot by itself evidence the construction skill.
A multiple-choice or recognition item can assess interpretation but does not elicit independent construction; include an actual drawing/placing step to assess 'translating'.

A snap-to-equal-width builder lowers drawing friction but can mask form errors; also observe free-hand or manual construction to check the learner can produce equal-width bars from a baseline unaided.
Optional interactions (sliding bars together, shading the difference, dragging bar heights) are illustrative aids, not required mechanisms; the learner must still state the subtraction or count.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim string is attributed to a gov.uk (England National Curriculum) URL but labelled as Common Core 2.MD.B.10 aligned with England NC Year 3; this cross-labelling was preserved as-is and not independently re-verified.

The legacy row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that dialogue 'offers nothing to construct'; these were softened — a conversation can support reasoning about a graph, and 3D is simply unnecessary for single-unit flat graphs rather than proven to add nothing. No comparative-efficacy claim is made.

Neither source directly supports the equal-width/common-baseline 'grammar' requirement as such; it is retained from the pedagogy best-practices as a conventional teaching point, not as a source-verified claim.
Worked example cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3 was checked and is correct; fish 4 and birds 2 bars were checked as consistent with the stated data.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how did you get how many MORE?' to check a difference was computed, not a height read
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'if I drew the dogs bar starting halfway up, would it still tell us 6? why not?' to probe the baseline
Ask 'how many chose cats AND dogs together?' to test put-together reading
Ask 'why must the bars be the same width?' to surface why height alone must carry the count
assess.correctAnswer: Interpreting: reads both bars against the scale and gives the DIFFERENCE (e.g. cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3), explaining the comparison. Translating: draws a fish bar to 4 and a birds bar to 2, equal width, rising from the baseline, correctly against the scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value instead of the difference between the two bars
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align the two bars and count the squares the taller one sticks up by; name 'how many more' as that gap, then re-ask
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives the cats value (9) rather than 9 − 6 = 3

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a bar's value off by one — counts gridlines rather than the value the top reaches, or reads a bar not starting at zero
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the bar top straight across to the scale number; check bars start at zero — a reading lapse to steady
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child's read value is consistently one out, or they count lines including the baseline

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws bars of unequal width, floating off the baseline, or unevenly spaced, so height no longer represents count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the grammar: equal-width bars from a common baseline, one square per unit; connect back to one unit = one item
errorPatterns.revealedBy: New bars don't start at the baseline, differ in width, or the picture-graph symbols vary in size

responseLevels.gap: Misreads the scale, gives the taller value for 'how many more', and draws malformed bars
responseLevels.full: Reads bars against the scale, computes 'how many more' as a difference, and constructs equal-width bars from the baseline to the right heights — moving fluently between graph and data
responseLevels.partial: Reads values and draws bars correctly with support, but the comparison is done by value not difference, or bar form needs reminding

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First: here is a bar graph of our class's favourite pets — how many MORE children chose cats than dogs, and how do you know? Then: here is the data for fish (4) and birds (2) — add those two bars to the graph correctly.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with representational fluency reads bar heights against the scale, computes the difference for 'how many more', AND constructs new bars to the right heights with correct form; a child without it reports the taller bar's value, misreads the scale by one, or draws bars off the baseline / unequal width. The construct step exposes whether height-means-count is truly understood.
